processing: A blend built on Georgian tea and substantially cut with imported Indian or Ceylon tea. The proportions are not documented.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest, since it was a commercial blend.
appearance_dry: Dark cut leaf, as is usual for a commercial black blend.
appearance_liquor: Reddish amber, likely deeper than straight Georgian tea because of the Indian or Ceylon share.
appearance_wet: Mixed dark brown cut leaf, as is usual for a blend.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting notes are recorded; Indian and Ceylon tea are sharper than Georgian, so a blend like this should be brisker than straight Georgian tea.

brewing.notes: A guide for a plain black blend: Western-style in a pot, shortened if it gets harsh.

vintage_note: A numbered commercial blend, sold without harvest year or season. No current production is documented, so an old pack is a curiosity rather than something to drink for pleasure.
description:
Tea No. 36 was a commercial black tea with Georgian tea as its base. Its identity lay in the blend and not in any one place or garden.

The Georgian base was substantially diluted with imported Indian or Ceylon tea, and the same was true of the tea called Bodrost. That mattered, because those teas are sharper and give more colour than Georgian alone.

The mix made it more popular than straight Georgian tea. The cost is that the stronger teas tend to cover the gentle Georgian character, so this is a tea for a strong everyday cup and not for studying a terroir.

No detailed recipe or tasting record is known, so anything sold under this number today may have little to do with the original.
history: Tea No. 36 is recorded among Georgian-based teas that sold better than pure Georgian tea thanks to imported Indian or Ceylon leaf. Little is documented about who blended it, when it appeared or when it ended.
